---
title: "Fixed quantile tiers"
subtitle: "3.1 · a simulated league, after the postrank theory book, ch. 9, 22 and 23"
description: "Posterior evaluation of directions stated by quantile groups of the estimates."
---

A quantile-tier rule cuts estimate order into nearly equal groups, ranking higher tiers above lower tiers and withholding same-tier pairs. Posterior probabilities evaluate its expected wrong directions and reporting risk.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Three tiers.** Three groups of 10 state 300 of 435 pairs (.690). Under the teaching posterior, expected wrong directions are 51.9 (.173 per stated pair) and risk is .181 at τ = .20.
- **Ten tiers, marks on.** Disclosure rises to 405 pairs (.931), while expected wrong directions rise to 89.4 (E/N = .221) and risk to .219; 197 stated pairs have error above τ (largest .802).
- **Four tiers.** Quantile positions give sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 and state 337 pairs (.775); **Method and formulas** shows the grouped binomial count without the equal-size shortcut.
- **Two tiers.** Two groups of 15 state 225 pairs (.517), leaving two within-tier triangles along the diagonal.
- **Thirty tiers.** Stating all 435 pairs in estimate order expects 102 wrong directions; with a single tier, E/N becomes “NA: no disclosure” and risk is .200.

<details>
<summary>Simulation and tie-handling notes</summary>

The example uses one set of estimates for thirty simulated units and independent normal posteriors based on a prior with mean 0 and SD .15. Changing τ alters the reporting loss and which stated pairs exceed τ without moving tier membership. In [Ranking states many claims](../uncertainty/ranking-claims.qmd), ranking by posterior means rather than raw estimates changes the expected wrong count. If an exact tie spans two tiers, postrank merges those tiers to keep tied units together.

</details>
